answer: Without the specific paper in view, the most likely answer is the standard incremental random-walk approach. The method precomputes and stores a set of short random walks starting from each node. When an edge is added or removed, only the stored walks that pass through the affected node(s) are identified and regenerated from the point of change onward, while the rest stay valid. Because a small graph change affects only a small fraction of these walks, the update cost scales with the number of affected walks rather than with the whole graph. The computational benefit is that the walk-based embedding or PageRank-style estimates can be kept current at a cost far below recomputing all walks from scratch. If the paper uses a different mechanism, this answer may not match it.
